# Prior Authorization Requirements and Prescription Fill Patterns Among Patients With Heart Failure

**Authors:** Amrita Mukhopadhyay; Samrachana Adhikari; Xiyue Li; Dhruv S. Kazi; Adam N. Berman; Ian Kronish; Carine Hamo; John A. Dodson; Rumi Chunara; Nathalia Ladino; Harmony R. Reynolds; Stuart D. Katz; Saul Blecker

## Abstract

Prior authorizations could hinder the filling of life-saving heart failure (HF) medications, such as angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is).

The aim of the study was to determine whether prior authorizations were associated with delayed or decreased filling for ARNI and SGLT2i.

This was a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record, pharmacy fill, and neighborhood-level data from a large, academic health system. We included patients with HF and a new prescription for ARNI or SGLT2i between April 1, 2021, and April 30, 2023, and assessed for presence of prior authorization requirement. Outcomes included days to first fill and never filling the prescription. Analyses were conducted using inverse probability weighting methods.

Among 2,183 patients, 12.2% (152/1,243) and 14.3% (165/1,150) had a prior authorization requirement for ARNI or SGLT2i, respectively. Patients requiring prior authorization tended to be younger, identify as non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic, have non-Medicare insurance, and have fewer comorbidities. In weighted models, patients requiring prior authorization took 3.03 (95% CI: 2.16-4.25) times longer to fill ARNI, 6.75 (95% CI: 4.44-10.3) times longer to fill SGLT2i, and were 2.23 (95% CI: 1.37-3.65) times more likely to never fill SGLT2i prescriptions (all P < 0.001).

Prior authorization requirements were more common for patients identifying as Black or Hispanic and were associated with decreased and delayed filling of ARNI and SGLT2i. Our findings highlight an important barrier to mortality-reducing, guideline-recommended medications for HF.

## Abstract

Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) and sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) substantially reduce mortality when added to a standard regimen for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF).1 However, over 80% of eligible patients are not prescribed these medications,2 and, even when prescribed, only 30 to 50% of patients take these medications regularly.3,4

One potential barrier to obtaining ARNI and SGLT2i among individuals prescribed these therapies is the need to obtain prior authorization prior to the initial prescription fill.5,6 This requires clinicians to provide medical justification for a medication and an insurance representative to approve the medication before it can be filled by the pharmacy. Prior authorization requirements are intended to reduce inappropriate utilization of expensive therapies. However, they may be harmful when applied to mortality-reducing therapies without generic alternatives, such as with ARNI and SGLT2i.6 In a national survey of physicians, 80% of respondents believed that prior authorization requirements delay care or lead to treatment abandonment.7 Moreover, in other clinical scenarios, prior authorization requirements have been associated with decreases and delays in prescription fills.8

Therefore, in this study, we sought to assess whether the presence of a prior authorization requirement was associated with decreased or delayed filling of prescriptions for ARNI and SGLT2i for patients with heart failure. We used a unique dataset that linked pharmacy fills with electronic health record order information, which has an advantage over administrative claims data by allowing for the assessment of prescription orders that were never filled and the inclusion of patients with different types of insurance plans.9 Further, we explored whether patients from minoritized racial and ethnic populations were at greater risk of prior authorization-associated decreases or delays in prescription fills.

## Methods

### Study design, data source, and participants

This was a retrospective cohort study conducted at a large academic health system with over 350 ambulatory practices and 4 hospitals. We utilized a linked dataset that contained information from both the electronic health record (Epic, LLC) as well as pharmacies and pharmacy benefit managers (Surescripts, LLC). This dataset allowed for the assessment of both prescription order information, via the health record, and prescription fill information, via pharmacy records.10 We then linked these data to neighborhood-level census information from the United States Census Bureau’s American Community Survey 2015 to 2019 using geocoded patient addresses (Geocodio, LLC). Patients were included if they: 1) had a diagnosis of heart failure (diagnosis codes11 are listed in Supplemental Appendix) or EF ≤40%; 2) were seen by a primary care provider or cardiologist between April 1st, 2021, and April 30th, 2023; and 3) were newly prescribed (ie, never previously prescribed) an ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) or a guideline-recommended12 SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). Patients were excluded if no prior authorization data were available, for example, due to unavailable pharmacy benefit plan information. All patients were followed until April 30th, 2024, to allow for a minimum of 365 days of follow-up. This study was approved by the NYU Grossman School of Medicine Institutional Review Board, and this report follows Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines.

### Exposure

The primary exposure was the presence of a prior authorization requirement. This was a binary variable generated at the time of prescription order using the Real-Time Prescription Benefit service (Surescripts, LLC),13 which obtains information from pharmacies, pharmacy benefit managers, and health plans, and links this information to the electronic health record. This variable was a prescription-level variable generated at the time of order entry and could change over time for the same patient and/or prescription (eg, if the prior authorization was approved, if the patient changed drug coverage plans, or if a different formulation not requiring prior authorization was prescribed). For patients with multiple prescriptions during the study period, the initial prescription order was used to assign the exposure. Prior authorization requirements were assessed separately for ARNI and SGLT2i.

### Outcomes

We assessed 2 main outcomes: the time to the first prescription fill and whether the patient never filled the prescription. Time to first fill was measured as the number of days between the first prescription order and the first medication fill within 365 days for that medication. Never filling the prescription was defined as no prescription fill within 365 days of the initial prescription order. A 365-day follow-up period was chosen to match the default time before prescription order expiration. We also conducted a sensitivity analysis using an outcome of no prescription fill within 90 days. For patients who died during the study period, outcomes were censored at the time of death, which was obtained from the electronic health record.

### Covariates

Demographic covariates were obtained from the electronic health record and included age, sex, race and ethnicity (Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, and non-Hispanic Other/Multiple/Unknown), preferred language (English or Other/Unknown), and primary health insurance type (Medicare, Medicaid, Commercial, or Other/Unknown). Clinical covariates were obtained at the time of prescription order and included the most recent EF (categorized as ≤40%, >40%, or missing), prior hospitalization or emergency department visit in the past year, and Elixhauser comorbidity index.14 Neighborhood-level socioeconomic status (nSES) was calculated using the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality nSES index,15 and categorized into quartiles, with missing nSES included as a separate category. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality nSES index uses variables from the American Community Survey to combine census-block information on crowding, property value, unemployment, poverty level, income, and education. Higher quartiles indicate higher nSES (ie, more socioeconomic resources).

### Statistical analysis

Analyses were conducted for ARNI and SGLT2i separately. Patient demographic, clinical, and neighborhood-level variables were tabulated by prior authorization requirement for each medication class. Unadjusted average time to first fill (for those who filled the medication) and unadjusted rates of never filling were compared using Student’s t-tests and chi-squared tests, respectively. To achieve balance in baseline characteristics between groups, we modeled the probability of prior authorization and used inverse probability weighting (IPW) for outcome analyses. Logistic regression models were created to assign the probability of prior authorization requirement based on patient baseline characteristics. These characteristics included age, sex, race and ethnicity, preferred language, most recent EF category, presence of any prior hospitalization or emergency department visit in the past year, Elixhauser comorbidity index, and nSES category. Missingness was included as a separate category for EF and nSES, as described above. Patient health insurance type was not included in probabilities and IPW weights due to violation of the positivity assumption, since a patient’s insurance plan directly dictated the prior authorization requirement. IPW weights were calculated as the reciprocal of the probability of prior authorization requirement and stabilized to preserve sample size. Standardized mean differences were used to assess balance between groups before and after weighting, with values close to or <0.1 suggesting evidence of covariate balance between the 2 groups.16

To estimate differences in time to first fill, we used IPW-weighted accelerated failure time models, with results expressed as a ratio between those who had prior authorization requirement and those who did not (time ratio) and 95% CI.17 Accelerated failure time analysis was chosen because the proportional hazards assumption required by the Cox model was not met. Model-predicted median (IQR) days to first fill were provided for interpretability. To assess the binary outcomes of never filling the prescription at 90 and 365 days, we used IPW-weighted robust Poisson regression models, which allowed for results to be expressed in terms of risk ratio (RR) and 95% CI with robust standard errors. To account for residual confounding by insurance type, we conducted additional sensitivity analyses for those with commercial insurance only; probabilities and IPW weights were recalculated within this group using the same methodology as the primary analysis. Significance tests were 2-tailed with alpha of 0.025 for Bonferroni correction to account for 2 primary outcomes.

Exploratory stratified analyses were repeated for the following prespecified subgroups: 1) above median nSES vs below median nSES, and 2) non-Hispanic Black vs non-Hispanic White. For stratified analyses, probabilities and IPW weights were recalculated within each prespecified subgroup, using the same methodology as the primary analysis. Analysis was conducted using accelerated failure time models and Poisson regression models, using the same methodology as the primary analysis, described above. Analyses were performed using R 4.4.3.

## Results

### Baseline characteristics

Among 3,315 patients with newly prescribed ARNI and 4,865 patients with newly prescribed SGLT2i, 37.5% (n = 1,243) and 31.0% (n = 1,150) of patients had available prior authorization data, respectively, and were included in the final analysis (total 2,183 patients) (Figure 1). Baseline demographic characteristics tended to be similar among patients with and without available prior authorization data. Higher proportions of patients with available prior authorization data also had available EF data, available insurance data, and a prior hospitalization or emergency department visit. Patients with prior authorization data also had a higher mean comorbidity index (Supplemental Table 1). A total of 4 patients in the ARNI cohort and 6 patients in the SGLT2i cohort died during the 365-day follow-up period. Prior authorization was required for 12.2% (152) of patients newly prescribed ARNI and 14.3% (165) of patients newly prescribed SGLT2i. Compared with patients who did not have prior authorization requirements, patients facing prior authorization requirements were younger, were more likely to be male, and were more likely to identify as non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic. Patients facing prior authorization requirements were more likely to have Medicaid or commercial insurance, and more likely to live in areas with lower nSES (Table 1). They were also more likely to have a lower comorbidity index and were more likely to have a prior hospitalization or emergency department visit in the past year. The proportion of patients with most recent EF ≤40% was similar between groups for ARNI (57.2% vs 57.8%), but was higher for those requiring prior authorization (52.1%) compared with those not requiring prior authorization for SGLT2i (36.9%). ### Delays in prescription fill

For ARNI, among those who filled the medication, average (SD) time to first fill was 26.4 (69.2) days for those requiring prior authorization, as compared with 13.1 (57.3) days for those not requiring prior authorization (P = 0.035). In IPW-weighted analysis, patients requiring prior authorization for ARNI took 3.03 (95% CI: 2.16-4.25) times as many days to fill the prescription, as compared to patients not requiring prior authorization (P < 0.001) (Central Illustration). For SGLT2i, among those who filled the medication, average (SD) time to first fill was 39.4 (84.0) days for patients requiring prior authorization, as compared with 16.4 (71.1) days for patients not requiring prior authorization (P = 0.004). In IPW-weighted analysis, patients with prior authorization, as compared with those without, took 6.75 (95% CI: 4.44-10.3) times as many days to fill the prescription (P < 0.001) (Central Illustration). Model-predicted median (IQR) days to first fill for those requiring prior authorization vs those not requiring prior authorization was 8.75 (2.39-32.05) vs 2.87 (0.78-10.50) days for ARNI and 30.9 (6.10-155.32) vs 4.56 (0.90-23.01) days for SGLT2i. In an exploratory IPW-weighted analysis including only patients with commercial insurance, patients with prior authorization took 5.32 (95% CI: 3.20-8.83) times as many days to fill ARNI and 5.77 (95% CI: 3.17-10.49) times as many days to fill SGLT2i as compared to those without prior authorization (all P < 0.001).Central IllustrationImpact of Prior Authorization on Filling Mortality-Reducing Heart Failure PrescriptionsaProbabilities for IPW analyses were generated from models that included the following baseline characteristics: age, sex, race and ethnicity, preferred language, neighborhood-level socioeconomic status quartile, most recent ejection fraction, Elixhauser comorbidity index, and prior hospitalization or emergency department visit within the past year. ### Decreases in prescription fill

For ARNI, the unadjusted rate of never filling the prescription at 365 days was 13.2% (20/152) for patients with a prior authorization requirement and 6.8% (74/1,091) for patients with no prior authorization requirement (P = 0.009) (Figure 2A). In IPW-weighted analysis, prior authorization requirement for ARNI at 365 days was associated with a 59% increase in the likelihood of never filling the prescription (RR: 1.59, 95% CI: 0.94-2.69), which was not statistically significant (P = 0.09). For SGLT2i, unadjusted rates were 21.8% (36/165) for patients with a prior authorization requirement and 11.9% (117/985) for patients with no prior authorization requirement (P < 0.001). For SGLT2i, prior authorization requirement for SGLT2i was associated with a 223% increase in the likelihood of never filling the prescription in IPW-weighted analyses (RR: 2.23, 95% CI: 1.37-3.65, P < 0.001). In a sensitivity analysis using a 90-day follow-up period instead of 365 days, the risk of not filling the prescription was higher for both ARNI (RR: 1.69, 95% CI 1.10-2.60, P = 0.02) and SGLT2i (RR: 2.27, 95% CI: 1.55-3.32, P < 0.001) (Figure 2B). In an exploratory analysis including only patients with commercial insurance, the risk of not filling the prescription at 365 days was higher for ARNI (RR: 3.26, 95% CI: 1.40-7.60, P = 0.006), but not statistically significant for SGLT2i (RR: 1.77, 95% CI: 0.86-3.64, P = 0.12).Figure 2Rate of Never Filling the PrescriptionPercent of patients never filling the prescription for ARNI and SGLT2i at (A) 365 days and (B) 90 days, by prior authorization requirement. aProbabilities for IPW analyses were generated from models that included the following baseline characteristics: age, sex, race and ethnicity, preferred language, neighborhood-level socioeconomic status quartile, most recent ejection fraction, Elixhauser comorbidity index, and prior hospitalization or emergency department visit within the past year. bSample sizes were 1,243 patients for ARNI and 1,150 patients for SGLT2i. ### Stratified analyses

The percentage of patients requiring prior authorization was higher for patients living in below median nSES areas as compared with above median nSES areas for both ARNI (13.6% vs 9.6%) and SGLT2i (15.1% vs 12.7%) (Table 2). Rates of prior authorization requirement were also higher for non-Hispanic Black patients as compared with non-Hispanic White patients for both ARNI (18.2% vs 9.2%) and SGLT2i (24.9% vs 10.7%). Across all nSES and race and ethnicity subgroups, having a prior authorization requirement was associated with increases in time to prescription fill for both ARNI and SGLT2i in IPW-weighted models (all P < 0.005) (Table 2). For SGLT2i, patients with prior authorization requirement were approximately twice as likely to never fill their prescription across all nSES and race subgroups in IPW-weighted models. ## Discussion

In this retrospective cohort study of patients with heart failure who were newly prescribed ARNI or SGLT2i, prior authorization requirements were more common for patients living in low nSES areas and those who identified as non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic, and were associated with substantial delays and decreases in prescription fill. Specifically, patients with prior authorization requirements took 3 times as many days to fill their prescription for ARNI, more than 6 times as many days to fill their prescription for SGLT2i, and were over twice as likely to never fill their prescription for SGLT2i. These associations were observed after IPW-weighted analyses to account for demographic, clinical, and neighborhood-level covariates and were observed across nSES and race and ethnicity subgroups. Our findings highlight a considerable impact of prior authorization requirements on access to mortality-reducing, guideline-recommended medications for heart failure.

Prior authorizations are commonly used to reduce costs for expensive medications by promoting the use of less expensive, generic alternatives. However, when applied to potentially life-saving medications with no generic alternatives, such as ARNI and SGLT2i, prior authorization policies may hinder timely, guideline-recommended treatment. In this study of patients with heart failure, we found that prior authorization requirements were associated with increases in time until and decreases in likelihood of prescription fill within 365 days. Our findings are consistent with similar studies in other clinical settings,8 including oncology,18 rheumatology,19, 20, 21 and gastroenterology,22 as well as investigations of region-wide changes in prior authorization policies,23, 24, 25 which also showed similar associations between these requirements and decreases or delays in treatment. Our study expands on this existing literature by redemonstrating this barrier in a contemporary, U.S.-based cohort for 2 mortality-reducing medications used to treat heart failure, a common and highly morbid condition that has a 5-year mortality of 40% to 60%.26 Moreover, we used a unique dataset that linked electronic health record and pharmacy fill data, which allowed us to include patients with multiple insurance types; to account for demographic, neighborhood-level, and clinical factors, such as EF; and to assess for prescriptions that were ordered and never filled—a key novelty in our work.

Importantly, we found that prior authorization requirements were more common for patients who identified as Black or Hispanic and lived in lower nSES areas. These findings suggest the potential for prior authorization requirements to exacerbate existing disparities in heart failure treatment and outcomes.27 Black patients and patients living in more resource-limited neighborhoods are more likely to experience, be hospitalized with, and die from heart failure.27, 28, 29 Moreover, Black patients and patients living in neighborhoods with lower socioeconomic resources are also less likely to obtain ARNI30,31 and SGLT2i.32,33 The cause of these disparities is likely multifactorial, including environmental, economic, provider-level, community-level, health systems-level, and cultural factors.34 Our findings demonstrate that barriers related to prior authorizations—a cost reducing strategy employed by insurance companies—are likely 1 additional component contributing to substantial inequities in cardiovascular care delivery.

The role of prior authorization requirements in health care likely extends beyond the associations we assessed in this study. For example, at the patient level, it is possible that frustrations with prior authorization requirements could lead to lower engagement with their health or with the health care system overall. In 1 survey, 83% of patients who had experienced a prior authorization reported a subsequent decrease in trust toward the health care system.35 On the provider level, clinicians may be less likely to prescribe medications if they are worried about the administrative and time burden related to prior authorization requirements. In a study using qualitative interviews of clinicians specifically regarding barriers to ARNI and SGLT2i prescribing for heart failure with reduced EF, a third of clinicians reported prior authorization as a hindrance to prescribing these medications.6 Future work quantifying associations between prior authorization requirements and patient adherence to other guideline-recommended therapies and on clinician prescribing practices will be critical to further elucidate the potential impacts of these policies.

### Study Limitations

This was a retrospective analysis of data from a single health system and may be limited in generalizability. Although our data source allowed for inclusion of information from multiple payers, there may be local or geographical differences—for example, prior authorization is not required by New York State Medicaid for ARNI or SGLT2i.36 Moreover, although our IPW approach achieved good balance on the included covariates, we could not account for unmeasured confounders, and there may be residual confounding by payer. For example, Medicare plans have previously been reported to have fewer prior authorization requirements for ARNI,5 which we also noted in our sample, and our finding of higher comorbidity burden among those without prior authorization requirement may reflect this. Of note, we conducted an exploratory analysis that included only those with commercial insurance, which also revealed similar findings. Due to the nature of our dataset, prior authorization data and EF data were only available for some patients, which may have introduced selection bias limiting the generalizability of our findings. Of note, patients with missing prior authorization data seemed to be more likely to be missing other data, such as EF, insurance type, or information on comorbidities or prior hospitalization. Despite these limitations in data availability, our dataset is unique in that it allows for the assessment of prescription orders that were never filled, a key requirement for this analysis. Mortality information was obtained from the electronic health record, which may not be complete. We did not have access to information on the granular details of the prior authorization process for each patient, such as if the prior authorization was initiated, if the prescriber responded, if the request was denied, and why, and therefore, could not ascertain whether a prescription was never filled due to the prior authorization requirement itself vs other clinical considerations. We also did not have prescriber information, such as prescriber demographics or practice characteristics. Subgroup analysis was exploratory, and effect modification by subgroup was not explicitly tested using interaction terms due to modest subgroup sample size. Prior authorization requirements may be justified if the drugs are frequently prescribed for conditions for which their use is not approved or indicated, such as if they were primarily directed at patients without reduced EF in whom the clinical benefits of ARNI and SGLT2i are less clear.12 Interestingly, we also found that prior authorization requirements for SGLT2i were more common for those with reduced EF, and we included the most recent EF in our IPW-weighted models. Moreover, the majority of patients requiring prior authorization were eventually able to fill the medication, suggesting that the medication was deemed to be appropriate for most patients in the study.

## Conclusions

We found that patients with prior authorization requirements for ARNI and SGLT2i were more likely to be Black or Hispanic and more likely to live in a lower socioeconomic status neighborhood. Patients with prior authorization requirements took substantially longer to fill their prescriptions and were less likely to fill their prescription at 1 year. These associations persisted after IPW-weighting for demographic, clinical, and neighborhood-level characteristics. Our findings highlight the considerable impact of prior authorization requirements on access to life-saving medications for heart failure.
